title: Bright Dawn project map

last_change.what: Above 1x, outlines are as wide on every side and smooth, on the nearer of two models only, at a sixth of their former cost at 4x. A glow the game blends over the 3D (as the star on the cliff) shows over it on the graphics hardware, not in a black box.

boxes.label: nds: the console around the processor

lines.text: Works: memory map, registers, interrupts, timers, DMA, math unit, cartridge, 2D engines, 3D geometry and renderer, display capture, buttons, touch.
Partly: second processor stand-in (4 of its services, the save chip kept in a file; no music sequences),
time (one cycle per instruction). The game runs to its name entry, built or interpreted.
Vulkan; 3D on the GPU up to 8x
sound is made, not played yet
window, paths, settings, frame clock, crash and hang notes

parts.now: Checks the ROM, reads its file system, archives and every kind of compression the game uses.
Decodes the menus' pictures and the game's font (NFTR) for the launcher. Textures, models and sounds: not yet.
Planned: replace game files without changing the ROM.

Translates 18,271 functions of the game's code, and the interrupt entry of Bright Dawn's own BIOS, to C++, on your computer, with interrupt polls and instruction counts. Where code puts its own return address in lr before a jump, that address is translated too, and so is the place a saved thread context is resumed at, and code whose address the program loads as a constant (its interrupt handler, for example).
Downloads its compiler (and Python on Windows) for the build and deletes it after. The downloaded compiler is not yet tried on a real build.
Builds, loads and runs: reaches the name entry like the interpreted game, about twice as fast (600 frames in 11 s instead of 24).

Runs translated code with the interpreter behind it. Interrupts are taken where translated code polls for them. Calls that never return no longer pile up until the program crashes (the Windows crash after about 7 minutes). Each run writes a log of the places run in the interpreter, with why.

The console model runs the game from the title screen to battles, with a save from about two thirds through the game. The game's save is kept between runs, also one made in the game; the console's language is a setting. The second processor's music player is written natively.

Both screens in one window, any size, stacked, side by side or the touch screen alone, sharp pixels with smooth edges. Drawn through Vulkan, or the system's renderer where there is none. 3D scenes by the graphics hardware at up to 8 times the DS's resolution, battles too, with vertices between the DS's pixels so that models move smoothly, on one screen or both, or by the processor. The 2D engines' pictures by the graphics hardware too, pixel for pixel as the processor draws them, except where a display capture needs the processor's. Outlines (original thickness, 1 pixel or off), shadows and fog as on the DS; at 1x the processor's picture, pixel for pixel, with the smoothing of polygon edges; above 1x outlines that meet the models' edges, as wide on every side and smooth, without the costly drawing by the DS's rules. The 2D stays at the DS's resolution: the game does not turn or scale it, so it would look the same drawn larger. Widescreen: not yet.
Music and sound effects play through your audio device (SDL 3), kept in step with the frames. Settings, Sound: on or off, and the volume.
Keyboard, any number of controllers, the mouse as the stylus. Keys and buttons can be bound in Settings, Controls.

The launcher's first page is Play and your save, on the game's page of saves, and a gear to the settings; its other pages look like the game's settings menu; all from your ROM. The setup before the first build is in the program's own look. Settings book, pause menu. Settings, Quality of life: Start skips the opening of a new game. Report a problem opens a filled-in bug form on GitHub. A Debug page switches on the frame log: what each frame costs, part by part.
Window, files, settings, frame timing, log, checksums. A crash is noted with where it happened; a game that stops finishing frames too.

Every change is built and tested on Linux and Windows; green changes on main become a pre-release. Its description gives the state first, then the big changes since the last one. Issue forms for bugs, a stuck game or wrong graphics, and wishes.
